If on the voyage there has been, or now is any one sick or dead on hoard, and in such case what was the dicasc according to his best judgment ? If all these questions are satisfactorily answered and in such a manner that the « aptain is willing to make Oath to them when required, and after the Crew and Passengers have shewn themselves on deck and evince a healthy appearance, the Physician or the deputy can then go on board, and if proper cleanliness is found to prevail, the Quarantine Flag can be hauled down and the vessel permitted to warp in among the other vessels and have free intercourse with these and the Land. The following Vessels will have to be placed under Quarantine

3T © & <S> 2 A?33, 1, Vessels arriving from places infected or suspected to be infected with Cholera although they have not had any cases of sickness or deaths by Cholera, but which on the passage have had communication with another vessel coming from infected or suspected places. The period for these vessels to lay quarantine is fixed at 5 Days, but to be calculated from the time this vessel bad the last communication or intercourse with the place,

suspected to be so, consequently all vessels arriving of which a great- j er number of days than the 5 prescribed have expired since they last had any communication or intercourse as above stated, shall be entirely exempted from quarantine. 2, Vessels which have had sick or deaths by Cholera on board. Quarantine fixed lor these are 5 days to be calculated from the time the sick or þÿdeceased bedding s and clotlie3 have been destroyed, or by washing, airing and fumigating have been disinfected and the vessel j by same process has also been cleans- 1 ed. If any individual should be attacked with Cholera before the expiration of the 5 days, the term of quarantine shall recommence, and continue until 5 days have expired that no Cholera exists. C, As long as the Cholera does not exist on shore no Cholera patient shall be landed and brought to the Hospital, nor any individual dying on board of that disease will be permitted to be intered on shore, but is to be carried outside the Reef at Christiansted, and at Fredericksted a considerable distance to the North of the Fort, and there to be sunk with Clothes and Redding, furnished with a sufficient quantity of weight. The Medicines which the Cholera patients may require on board, | as well as other supplies, will be furnished by the Quarantine Pliysician and the Board of Health during the time the quarantine lasts. D, From vessels having had the Cholera on board, not even the clothes of the Crew or Passengers who are in

health, shall be permitted to be sent on shore to be washed before they have been washed on board in salt water and dried in the air. For the violation or neglect of the rules prescribed by this regulation the punishment is according to the Ordinance of 8th February 1805 and of 19th June 1831 forfeiture of fines varying according to the degree of culpability from $3. 20 to $640, and in certain specified cases of intentional violation of particularly aggravating nature, forfeiture of life. The New Trench Minister-at-War. þÿ Public opinion, that is, the opinion of newsmongers in Paris, seem to be rather puzzled than divided by the appointment of General Schramm to the War Department. The only thing that seems to be admitted on all hands is that the new Minister of War is a man of much decision. lie distinguished himself in particular in the repression of the Republic insurrections that troubled the first years of the reign of Louis Philippe, and was for his decided conduct in 1832 made General of Division and Peer of France. He was also Chef du Personnel de la Guerre when Marshal Maison was Minister of War, in 1837.

We give the following slight sketch ol the past career of the newly appointed French Minster of War Gen. Schramm as he appears to excite great notice from ail parties, it may prove interesting to our readers. þÿ General Schramm, the new Minister of War, is 61 years of age. lie entered the service at a very early age, and was promoted to the rank of lieutenant in 1805. In the following year, as a reward for his bravery in different affairs he received the Cross of the Legion of Honour, and in 1806 to 1807 was aid-ilccamp to his father General Schramm. þÿ In 1307 he was made a captain by the Emperor. After distinguishing himself greatly in different campaigns in the intermediate grades, he arrived at the grade of general of brigade when he was only 24 years of age. On the return of the Emperor from the Island of Elba, General Schramm was appointed to the command of the department of the . Vlaine-ct-Loire, bathe surrendered these .unctions to take part in the defence of Paris in June, 1815. From that time until 1823 General Schramm remained unemployed, but in 1828 he was appointed to the first division of the camp of St. Omer. In 1830 he commanded the department of the Bas-Rhin, and in 1831 went with the expedition to Belgium in command of the lirst brigade of the division of infantry. In 1832 lie was made a Lieutenant-General, and in 1839 he commanded the third division of the army of Algeria. In 1811 he was appointed to the command in thief of\that army, and retained the command until

the arrival of General Bugeaud as Governor-General. In 1848 he was appointed president of the commission of reorganisation of the corps des ofliciers de sante militaircs, and since 1649 he has been president of the committee of infantry.

General Cavaignac. þÿ Considerable discussion is going on in the French papers as to the probable course that may be taken by the military members of the Left in the Assembly in case of an attempt at a revision of the Constitution, or the prolongation of the powers of the President. By some it is contended that General Cavaignac would place himself

AT 2 3 at the head of a party to resist vi et armis, if necessary, any attempt at revision, unless in the manner, and at the period, prescribed by the Constitution. There are few who will deny the title of Gen. Cavaignac to public gratitude for the eminent services be rendered in days of j danger ; and his ability as a parliamen- i tary debater is equally admitted. But j it must be a calumny on the General to presume that, in case the nation, by the voice of its representatives elected freely by universal suffrage, and in whose hands, to use the language of the day, the popular sovereignty has been deposited for a period, demand the revision of a Constitution so full of defects, he will enrol himself amongst mere revolutionists, and become the General-in- Chief of insurgents in arms against the National Assembly, of which lie himself . is a member. General Cavaignac will, there is no doubt, express his opinion on the question of revision, as on all other questions brought forward in the Assembly ; but it is very doubtful that, with the memory of li is own treatment of the insurgents of June still fresh, General Cavaignac would himself become þÿ what armed resistance to the decision of the Assembly would unquestionable make him. It is stated, however, in well-informed quarters, that there is no intention of mooting the question of the revision of the Constitution until alter May, 1851, the period prescribed by the j Constitution itself. If such be the case, nothing can be said against the legality

of the measure. (From llic Morning Chronicle of 14th November.,) The changes which have taken place in the policy of the Prussian Government have been so rapid and so unexpected as equally to defy calculation and conjecture. On the 2d inst. the advisers of the Prussian Court agreed, though unwillingly enough, to accept the terms proposed at the conference at Warsaw ; and the resignation of M. Von Radowitz was the consequence of the abandonment of the system which had been pursued by that statesman since his accession to office. On the 5th it was suddenly determined to call out a military force sufficient to delay or to nullity tin practical results of the stipulations of Warsaw. A corresponding attitude was maintained by the commanders of the Prussian troops, and it appeared as if nothing could avert a conllict, should the Diet at Frankfort persist in giving effect to its resolutions. That danger was, however, put an end to by a new decision of t he Prussian Government; for, on the 7th, their policy for the third time underwent a change, and all intention of resistance was apparently abandoned. The demands of Austriaþÿ urged though they have been in a manner calculated to wound deeply the pride of the Prussian people are it is said, to þÿ be complied with in every particular: and consequently the only result of the warlike determination of the Cabinet of Berlin has been, to provoke to the ut- ! most the national feelings of the people, summoning them to contemplate, with

arms in their hands, the annihilation of all the projects to which Prussian ambition had been directed bv the Ministers of the Crown, and to which Priu sian honour had been pledged by tin word of the King. It is already wins pored that the evacuation of Hamburg, and the withdrawal of the army of occupation from Baden, have taken place m obedience to the commands of Austria, supported by the authority of the Czar. Nothing is wanting to complete tho humiliation to which Prussia has been brought by the unjustifiable aggressions i of her Government, and by the undignified manner in which she has been obliged to recede, step by step, from every position which she had occupied, either from considerations of political advantage, or with a view to military operations. Such, according to the latest accounts, is the posture of affairs. It would be rash to augur a pacific. olution of the German question from he last phase presented by the changeful politics of Berlin. It is more likely
to increase than to diminish the popular Landwehr has so forcibly stimulated.

for the Cabinet of Berlin to maintain an armed peace, and to permit the affairs of Germany to be exclusively managed by the Diet at Frankfort, supported by the troops of the southern states. Even in the first instance, to recede from the pretensions put forward by Prussia involved sacrifices hard to be borne by a military nation ; but, after the challenge which the King offered to his enemies by appealing to his people, it is a degradation which the Prussians will scarcely submit to, in spite of the danger to 'hemselves and to Germany. Such are

ill-advised schemes, of the violation of the Electorate of Hesse, and of the hostile and haughty bearing of Prussia in all discussions concerning the reconstruction of Germany. The difficulties of the crisis might have been in some measure diminished if greater consideration had been shown

and for the feelings of the Prussian people. But no interval lias been suffered o elapse between the conference at Warsaw and the prosecution of active measures ; and thus the carrying out of he agreement made between the cabinets has had the appearance of intimidation and coercion. The more suspicious of the Liberal party have detected m these operations the promptings of j country, the historical ally of Prussia, Russia, and they have inferred, with ome appearance of reason, that the sudden activity of the Austrian Govern- j zenberg. An army will he sent by the inent proceeded from a well-grounded confidence in the moral and material support of that power. To what extent the Czar may have engaged himself 1 will not, it is said, interfere ; and, in to support Austria in her present struggle is at best but matter of conjecture, but we cannot fail to acknowledge the enormously increased influence which has accrued to Russia from the disunion of Germany. The suspension of arms to which Prussia has consented with so much reluctance, and which Austria seems scarcely to have desired, is the recommendation, or rather the injunction, of a foreign power, which is the natural enemy of the one, and the scarcely less dangerous friend of the other. States which hold a high rank in civilised Europe have argued their cause before the Emperor of Russia, and have not blushed to accept his decision. From what has taken place during the last few weeks, it might fairly be concluded that the Government of

France and England have ceased to exercise the slightest influence in Continental politics. That the former should have taken a comparatively unimportant part in these discussions is perhaps not very surprising ; and the paragraphs of the President's Message respecting the foreign policy of the Republic seem to be almost an apology for the weakness of the French Government. From the St. Thomas Times, Dec. 14. The R. M. steamer þÿ Trent," arrived here yesterday morning; she has brought our usual intelligence from Europe. The Trent did not leave Southampton, until the afternoon of the 18th ult. þÿ the 17th, her appointed day for proceeding to sea, falling on a Sunday. She experienced very bad weather, and after being out about 48 hours was obliged to put into Torbay for shelter. She remained there the better part of a day, and as soon as | the weather permitted, she prosecuted her voyage. During the greater part of | the passage she had to contend against adverse winds and heavy seas. This will account for her delay as steamers cannot make much way in heavy seas owing to the inequality of surface presented for their paddles to act on ; often only one wheel taking effect in the water while the other is playing in the air. þÿ The most way steamers will make, under such circumstances, is from 1A to 2 knots an hour. The Trent on her arrival had still 3 tons of coal left, and it is satisfac tory to be able to state that, even with I have heavy the nothing to record in the way of weather she experienced we accident or injury sustained by her; a pretty strong proof of what those vessels are capable of enduring, and of the absolute safety for conveyance they present. She brings out about 120 passengers.

From the New York Herald. Intentions of Russia. The following information has been communicated from a semi-official source, and we understand that one of our first bankers at þÿl arishas received similar information from his correspondents at ! Vienna and Berlin : þÿ The Emperor of Russia makes no concealment of his dissatisfaction at the conduct of the Prussian cabinet in the affair of the Duchies. He lias told the Count de Brandeburg, the Prussian # , NIinister, that he cannot see the policy of his cabinet, in throwing obstacles in the way of the settlement of the question, and seeking to cover a departure from honesty and good faith liy a dispute about the constitution of the Diet of Frankfort, which has ratified the treaty of peace, lie expressed himself ! in equally strong terms on the Hesse question, which lie said could have been j settled at once by the adoption of the ancient arbitral system of Prussia, had it not excited the people on the one 35, ! hand, and irritated the sovereign on the other. The menace of preventing the intervention of the Diet by force of arms, was strongly blamed by the Emperor ; and, in conclusion, lie declared that, if the ministers of the King of Prussia should continue to excite the revolutionary feeling in Germany, they would be guilty of little less than treason, for flic destruction of the monarchy, or, at least, the deposition of the reigning sovereign could alone he the result. It is possible that there may he some exaggeration in this account; hut no

doubt can bo entertained of the spirit in which the Emperor of Russia addressed the Prussian Minister, for the subject was the topic of general conversation at Warsaw, among the officers of the Czar. But the most important fact is ihe reported refusal of the Emperor ot Russia to receive his brother-in-law, the King of Prussia, at Warsaw. It appears that M. Radowitz had boasted that the Emperor had positively adopted the cause of Prussia against Austria. This reached the ears of the Emperor at the very moment when he received a letter from the King of Prussia, expressing liis intention to visit him at Warsaw, it it would be agreeable to the Emperor to receive him. The Emperor replied that under the circumstances, it would be more agreeable to him to have the visit deferred, and immediately sent an autograph letter to t lie Emperor ot Austria, inviting him to Warsaw, as it was high time to bring the German question to a solution. In order that it might not be supposed that Russia regarded Austria as her vassal and that the Emperor of Austria was going to Warsaw to receive instructions as to his future conduct, the Czar took every means of making known that he had invited his ally, and to prove this the more, resolved to meet him on the frontier þÿ this act of courtesy being intended to prove that it was as an ally and an equal that wished to receive the young sovereign. »> þÿ ¬> From the Northern Whig, Belfast, November 12, 1850.

FRANCE. The President of the French Republic has issued a decree dissolving the Society of the 10th of December, and not before its time, if what is said regarding it be true ; for we are informed by The Dehats that, on the 29th ult., twenty-six members of this Society held a sitting, at which a scheme was discussed for the assassination of M. Bupin, the President of the Assembly, and General Changarnier, the Commander-in-Chiel of the army. Lots were actually drawn for the two individuals upon whom should fall the atrocious act of committing the murderous deeds, one of whom expressed his entire willingness to perform the task assigned to him, while the other maintained a perfect silence. The day for the execution of the diabolical plot was left to be determined at a future meeting. This alleged conspiracy formed the principal subject of conversation on Friday, among the various political parties in Paris; but a positive contradiction to the story has been given by Cartier, Prefect of Police. A Cabinet Council was held on Friday, when the þÿPresident s Message was taken into consideration, but it is not to be finally agreed upon until to-morrow (Sunday). At the municipal elections of Euroque (Eot et Garonne), and at La Palisse (Allicr), the Conservatives obtained the majority. The Cmutitutionnel is very indignant tiiat the English peo-

<B&<D XZ ple should manifest such determined , opposition to the late edicts of the Pope, in appointing an Archbishop and Bishops to rule over them. A duel, with swords, took place, on Wednesday, in Meudon Wood, between M. Charles Hugo and J. M. Charles Vicnnot, both of whom are connected with the press. The former was wound- ! ed in the knee, but not seriously. Another duel was to have taken place, on Tuesday, between M. Roqucplan, the Director of the opera, and M. Fiorenti- j no relative to an article which had been published by the latter in The Corsunr ; but the intervention of friends rendered | the meeting unnecessary. Incendiary fires still continue in the ! Provinces.

Intelligence has arrived here, from the Prussian headquarters, that a skirmish took place last evening, between the Bavarian and Prussian outposts, on the banks ot the small stream which separates the Fulda from the Hanau district. The General commanding the Prussians desired that the stream should serve as a demarcation line between the opposing corps ; but the Bavarians declined, saying that they knew of no other line of demarcation than that of the Confederation; and, j adding action to the word, pushed on. þÿ Whereupon the Prussians opened their fire, and the Bavarians withdrew to the opposite bank. Great anxiety is felt to ascertain whether this affair will lead to further consequences. It is reported, . this evening, that M. de Radowitz has been sent lor to resume office. This i suggests the question, whether the reserve men in the Holstein army will not be allowed to remain '< Probably they will, as Prussia does not appear to be scrupulous as to means or ends. BERLIN. Our Berlin correspondence is of the 5th and Oth inst. It contains the confirmation of the intelligence of the death of Count Brandenburgh, and announces the important fact that, at a Council held at noon on the same day, the Cabinet decided on issuing the order it negatived when proposed by M. Von Radowitz, for placing on a war-footing the whole of the Prussian army, and calling out the Landwehr. The cause of this order is stated to be the fact that Prussia has been called on by Austria, in the name of the Confederation, to withdraw her troops from llessc. The funds of ! the Berlin Bourse fell on the announce- ment of the death of the President of the Ministry. From the Belfast Northern Whig, Nov. 28. Great Fire in Fredericton. þÿ I write in excessive baste. Our city has been desolated by the most terrific fire which, taking our population into account, has ever taken place in this Province. Upwards of one-half of the city is burnt, ere tinglteste forend lste Jannar 1831 j ! including a large portion of our best buildings and places of business, and the spacious Wesleyan Church and parsonage. The fire broke out about two þÿo clock in a barn near this church, and, before any assistance could be rendered, it was on fire, and with great difficulty the organ was taken to pieces and got out, with cushions, books, Ac.; but within hall-an-hour the llames wreathed spire, which, with the ponderous bell, into the midst of the burning heap. The fire then crossed Carleton-street, and drove rapidly on in I every direction, particularly among the thick cluster of stores in Queen-street, thence down to Regent-street, burning

i þÿo clock, at least 200 houses were burnt Gouvernemcntet for tic dansk- vcstin- j or on fire, and then by great exertion its progress was stopped. About 3,000 people are this evening houseless. The Catholic Chapel was on fire, but has been saved. The calamity is awful, as ruin must be the result to hundreds. þÿ The insurances were considerable. The Wesleyan Church was insured in the for 000/., and the organ for 100/. Other insurances on private property are considerable. The time, however, was unfavourable, as our merchants bad just got in their fall stocks, and, as a great deal is burnt, their insurances will be but a small compensation. The Central-office has lost heavily, of course, and so, also, have the foreign offices. The whole city seems to be in ruins. I look down and see nothing but long ranges of chimneys, surrounded by burning heaps, where, a few hours ago, hundreds of comfortable dwellings and stores existed. I cannot þÿ dare not þÿ attempt to realise the consequences. While I write (ten þÿo clock), tight the fire is still burning þÿ immense quantities of furniture, goods, Ac., are lying exposed, and hundreds of our citizens are in the streets, striving to look after the remnant of their property. What the houseless people are to do I know not. It is now almost Winter, and the means of accommodation cannot he furnished. All classes of people were at work þÿ the Governor, the Bishop and all sorts and conditions of men. þÿ St.John,

Sounding Boards for Pultits. þÿ I would suggest to the architects of sacred edifices, writes Mr. Webster, the Professor of Oratory to the Royal Acacanopies of pulpits should be formed of strained sheepskin, and inserted into a wooden frame (the skin to be painted to imitate the grain of the wood) and then suspended from the ceiling. By the adoption of this improvement, a great increase of reverberation may be a quired, and the voice of the preacher would be heard distinctly in the remotest part of the Church or Chapel, without exhausting physical þÿpower. Experimental Trip of the Gemini Iron Twin Steamer. þÿ Tuesday an experimental voyage was made by an iron steamer of a novel construction, to test, the practicability of giving greater accommodation to passengers, with equal speed in a vessel of low tonnage and of a very small draught of water. The vessel in question is called the Gemini, and is, in fact, two iron boats joined together and having the propulsive power in the centre in the shape of one gigantic paddle-wheel. It had alway been found that the concentration of what is technically called the backwater, » c., the reaction caused by the rotation of the paddle-wheel in the centre of the body to he moved, was a serious obstacle to progress, as by its constantly surging up, it seriously impeded the motion of the wheel. This defect, the patentee of the present vessel (Mr. Peter Borrie) has sought to remedy by making his two vessels, as it were, sections of one, such sections, by their division and the intervention of the paddle-wheel, giving a greater amount of deck-room than in vessels with external paddle-wheels, and greater steadiness of motion than could be obtained ur.der the old system, while the peculiar construction of their inner bilge diminished the chance of friction with the water. Another, and most important point to be achieved by the new construction, was the avoidance of any lateral disturbance of supporting fluid, so as to adapt the vessel to narrow river or canal navigation, where the

motion of a steamer is usually found to wash away the banks. With respect to the experiment of Tuesday, the appearance of the decks on going aboard proved that the first object had been achieved. The decks were as those of a line-of-battle ship, and would, wc believe, easily accommodate 000 or 700 pe.sons. Of the steadiness and safety of the vessel there cannot be any doubt, the breadth of beam securing the oner while the division of the hulls into watercompartment makes the other certain. Her speed is, however, still an undecided question. On þÿTuesday voy- s age she was more than once passed by the ordinary Gravesend steamers, and took two hours (against tide) to go from Blackwall to the Terrace-pier. As far as the canal problem is concerned, the experiment was completely successful- On the whole the experiment was satisfactory. A reasonable amount of speed (in smooth water) was obtained, perfect steadiness of motion was exhibited, and an amount of deck-room was obtained equal to that on board steamers constructed on the ordinary model of nearly double the tonnage. We were informed by the patentee that these results have been obtained at about two thirds the usual cost of construction, and at less than onehalf the ordinary consumption of fuel. The length of the Gemini is 140 feet breadth on deck, 21 feet; combined tonnage, about 50 tons ; and draft of water, 2J feet. She was constructed by Messrs. Robinson and Russell, of þÿMillwall. Fa virtue of the þÿGovernment o s rdinance of 4th May 1841), the inhabitants of this island will soon he, again, called upon to vote for new members for the liurgher Council: the manner in which members have, heretofore, been elected, evinces that, it is considered a matter of little consequence who are chosen, whereas, in reality, it is of essential importance, provided the members act up to their duty. Though it be true that these duties are not minutely defined by any positive law, yet the Edict of 8th April 17G8 together with the regulations which exist in the Mother Country for the communes, sufficiently point out the position which ought to be assumed by this body. In the election, therefore, of new members, the various interests of the island ought to be represented; hitherto that of the Planters has principally, if not entirely, predominated; it would, also, be advisable to elect one or two members conversant with law ; and as the mercantile interest should also be represented, one or two merchants ought, consequently, to be chosen, above all, the delegates should be men of liberal and independent minds, unconnected by office, or otherwise, with Government, and on the other hand, let the election of such be avoided who are blindly opposed to the executive, otherwise it can never be expected that the liurgher Council and the Government can go hand in hand in furtherance of the welfare of the country. There are individuals who, from vanity, aspire to be members of this body, without pos-

sessing the necessary acquirements, and tind such who are weak enough to foster it by voting for them ; now as such cannot but cut a ridiculous figure among their colleagues, and perhaps might tend to bring the Council into disrepute, if not contempt, votes should not be thrown away upon those w hose deficiences may have so pernicious a tendency. ( Limerick Chronicle) nice, grieved to record a most calamitous loss of life shipwreck on our immediate coast, and deeply grieved to add, that all the victims are of this country. The Edmond, of London, John Wilson, master, a barque of 399 tons register, was early
Lsq., of Limerick, to convey passengers to New York. Total number embarked, 195; distinguishing 171 steerage and 21

The crew consisted of the master, two mates, and 18 hands, total number of souls on board, 230. The ill-fated ship sailed from the quays of Limerick on Friday þÿsc nnight, and proceeded to It was a the land, would

till Sunday, when she went down to Carrigaholt, where she till morning, when, the weather being favourable, she proceeded outwards. After being thirty miles at sea the wind headed, and blew a terrific gale, which carried away all the þÿship canvass, s and she was driven back into Kilkcc bay without any damage until she struck on the rocks under þÿSikes lodge, at halfpast 11 at night, and became a total wreck at 3 next morning. Out of 230 souls, 120 are saved, as far as can at present be ascertained. Forty-seven dead bodies have been washed in, The only person of the crew lost is the carpenter, and the majority of the passengers lost arc women and children. It is a miracle how the vessel got into the bay, the only ship that ever was seen to there, the passage being so very narrow, and, even to those acquainted with it at all times, most dangerous ; and yet, had the tide been the ebb, instead of coming in, every soul on board would have been saved ! The appearance of the catastrophe from the shore was indescribably agonizing, The shrieks of the passengers could be heard over the terrific roar of the sea, and of the winds, which continued to blow with resistless fury. Wave after wave washed the ill-fated ship till it completely swamped her ; but every effort that could be made was carried into effect to rescue the passengers from their heart-rending position. The following letter from Mr. Russell, of Kilkcc, is descriptive of this awful calamity : þÿ þÿ I shall endeavour to give you a par-

ticular account of the loss of this unfortunate vessel. It was about half-past eleven þÿo clock last night that I got out of bed to fasten the windows of our bedroom, shaken by the pitiless storm ; on looking out what was my horror to see before me, within about a hundred vards, a large vessel aground outside the rocks. It was low water ; I cannot describe my feelings : I knew that all in her were doomed to destruction, and, as 1 then believed, not a soul could be saved. At first there was no appearance of any living person on board, but as soon as we made our appearance with a light,

sjt <©3:1 2: a ti 3 I there was one burst of horrid agony for assistance. I sent at once to the Coast Guard and persons in the neighbourhood þÿ also to the village for aid. Where the vessel first lay there was no earthly by rose, which saving chance of it did a soul, but as the tide with terrific fury, she drifted in close to the Black Rock opposite our house (Mr. þÿSykes s),where the men usually bathe in summer. þÿ An When she got there the sea made terrilast month chartered by John þÿM Donnell, ble breaches over her, but still she bore it bravely. The Captain a noble fellow, as you will by-and-by learn þÿ ordered the weather-rigging of the foremost, cabin passengers, including þÿchildren. the only one then standing, to be cut. þÿ By this move the passengers and crew were offered some assistance to laud on the rock. To picture the state of the sea while coming on the rock, and from thence to be impossible. Scattery Roads, where the vessel lav breaking over the rocks, so as to make regular succession of seas it all but miraculous how even those lay Monday that were saved got along the rock. þÿ There is no doubt but that for the noble intrepidity and self-devotion of the < 'oast Guard, and an extra assistant, not one hall ot those that were saved could ever have got access to the rock, washed as it was by such sweeping sen. I and my servant were the only two who went down on the rock to assist these noble fellows. By the hands of these four fellows 100 souls were rescued from a watery grave. When the tide rose it

was perfectly impossible to land any more of the passengers on the rock ; and in a very short time the vessel broke up and parted midships. Several tried then to get on the rock, but were washed oil' at once ; the remainder held on the afterpart of the wreck, in which there could not be less than fifty souls þÿ this part containing poop deck and stern post, and some of the ufterpurt of the vessel was torn by the þÿl urv ot' the sea from the forepart, and drifted into the strand. It was at this moment the gallant captain and his mate, who so ably stood by their passengers, and who could not be prevailed on to desert them, were washed off the poop, and wonderful to say, got sale to land by the beach. Three other passengers were equally fortunate þÿ one of them was a woman whom the captain was the means of saving. All was now ever, and the melancholy duty remained of collecting the bodies of these poor victims. From all I can collect, there was no fault or blame to be laid to the capþÿtain s charge. He had every stitch of canvass blown away in the storm, so lie could only lay to the drift under bare poles. As yet only 45 bodies have been found. The actual loss of life cannot be ascertained for a few days, until we learn the names of the survivors. As yet 120 have answered. The bay is covered with fragments of the wreck. þÿ Nothing could exceed the brutal, and I regret to say, successful efforts of some people to plunder whatever they could lay their hands on ; they actually strip-
ped the clothes from the dead bodies, together with, of course, any money in them, which latter, it is supposed, was

considerable. It was impossible for us to protect or check those depredators. There were only four water guards and three police, who were up all the previous night, and could not be expected to protect the property on such a long line of beach. This evening a strong force has arrived, but they have come loo þÿlate. eye witness states that the sufferings of the poor survivors and their grief were truly heartrending. Parents without their children þÿ children without their parents þÿ many without clothes y and, with very few exceptions, all were wholly destitute, their little effects, having been entirely lost, and all the n sources they possessed in the deep. þÿ Wave alter wave washed ashore the bodies of the dead, and augmented the horrors and agony of the scene. Every house in Kilkee w as converted into an hospital ; all the available resources of the village were putin immediate requisition. John l inn, the carpenter of the illfi'tcd Edmond, a native of Limerick, displayed extraordinary energy and humanity to the wretched sufferers on board, lie was instrumental in saving the lives of 15 persons, and had only gone below to secure his working chest, when the vessel parted amidships, and he unfortunately perished, lie has left a wife and four children to deplore his loss. On the 21st an inquest was held on 58 bodies of those who perished by the wreck. Verdict þÿ drowned, by the loss of the barque Edmond, and that no blame was to be attributed either to the master or crew.

Sinuui.au Discover v of a Brig Sunk Nine Years Ago. þÿ About nine years ago, as the .Alary Scott a Liverpool brig, laden with copper ore and a general cargo, and having on board a large quantity of specie, was returning from Valparaiso, she was ran into about five miles east of Point Lynns, by an American ship called the Brooklyn, and the result was, that the Alary Scott sunk in deep water and six or seven persons on board perished. Some time afterwards the brig Parana, outward bound for Montreal, was ran down by the Iron Duke, and sank between Ormsheud and Point Lynas. No traces of either vesdiscoverable until about three weeks ago, when a Liverpool fisherman, named Richard Price, whilst trolling near to Point Lynas, found that bis net bad become entangled to something beneath the surface of the water, and, on examination, discovered that it had caught in the wreck of a vessel. It is not positively known with which of the brigs the net became entangled : but it. is supposed that it is the Mary Scott ; and there is little doubt that it is witli one of the vessels, as no others are known to have gone down of late years in that locality. The þÿGovernment s Resolution of 19th December last, which will be found in another part of this taper, prescribes the following rules for the delivery of Medicine to the Poor of both towns, at the expense of the Land Treasury : þÿ þÿ 1, Every physician is authorised to prescribe medicine from the apothecary, at the expense of the Land Treasury, if there is absolute necessity for it, anil t he patient declares that he is unable to procure medirine in any other way, yet so, that every prescription for the poor he written in a legal form with the day, date, for whom, also with the word þÿ pauper, and that the physician strictly prescribes, according to circumstances, the cheapest medicines, and make use of the pharmacopea danica, or if possible, the pharmacopea pauperem. þÿ 2, Those persons who enjoy pension from the Land Treasury, shall he entitled to medicine gratuitously ; but others have, (before the medicine agreeable to the prescription can be obtained at the expense of the Land Treasury) to repair to the master of police or a member of the poor commission, who, upon finding nothing to prevent the sick person from obtaining medicine gratuitously, provides the prescription with the necessary guarantee for its acceptance One prescription provided with this guarantee is valid for all the others, that may he required, during the continuance of sickness of the same person. 3, The apothecaries will be obliged to send in their accounts monthly, for the medicines so delivered, with a statement
of to whom and by order of what physician these medicines were delivered. The original prescriptions must be num hi red and þÿattached.

DENMARK AND THE DUCHIES. The troops of the German Confederation are now steadily advancing to the frontiers of the Duchy of llolstein, and have probably crossed the Elbe at this moment, for the purpose of putting an end to the usurped authority of the insurrectionary Government of Kiel and of stopping that effusion of blood which has been so wantonly caused, even within the last few days, in open defiance of the laws of humanity, the faith of treaties, and the will of Europe. Since it lias been found necessary to resort to the last expedient of a military intervention for the purpose of crushing this stiffed- necked rebellion, þÿ the Danish anny having been restrained from crossing the Eyder by its own punctilious respect for the territory of Germany þÿ we are gratified that this demonstration should be made by the lawful Federal Power which the King of Denmark lias repeatedly invoked, and that Germany should be foremost in repairing the breach she herself had made. This occurrence is a great triumph of reason and right over the sallies of passion and the aggressions of a revolution, disguised in the popular colours of German nationality. Upwards of four years have elapsed since we first had occasion to examine the connexion of Denmark and the Du cities. The question was then but little known to Europe, and it had been grossly misrepresented by the German press in the pay of the Duke of Augustenberg. We formed our opinions from motives perfectly disinterested, but on strict, grounds of right ; and we have never

seen reason to depart a hair's breadth from the position we took up in September. 18-16. On the contrary, as the statesmen of Europe, and the leading organ of the continental press, beyond the reach of the German mania on tins subject, successively pursued this inquiry, they arrived with singular unan unity at the same conclusions. A prodigious revolution occurred in France, yet General Cavaignac and Louis Napoleon pursued on the Danish question the identical policy of M. Guizot. þÿ From the Emperor of Russia to the French Republic every Power not actually engaged in the contest recognized the positive rights of tbe Crown of Den mark, and even Lord Palmerston, who appears to have thought for a considerable time that the subject was one of secondary importance, or that Denmark was a cheap sacrifice to a German revolution, did at last zealously adopt the same view which we had so long pressed upon his notice, and, by the conclusion of the Protocol of London, insured a certain, though tardy, termination of this war. We admit, however, that if was worth some delay to bring the German Cabinets, which were the most guilty parties in this transaction, to a distinct recantation of their ofi'ence. If Germany has a right to include the Duchy of llolstcin within its Federal territories the lawful Government of Hoi- Heir ha-- an indefensible ejnim to Fede-

a ral support; and the conduct ol the German States was doubly base, because, when this insurrection broke out, they were bound to interfere, if called upon, not to instigate, but to put an eiij to it. That call has at last been made, heard, and obeyed ; and, though Denmark has the same right to march Danish regiments into Holstein which Austria has to march her Italians and Hungarians, and Prussia her Poles, into Germany, it may tend to promote a peaceful termination that this occupation should be made in the name of the German Powers. The Assembly at Kiel decided on the Tlth, by a majority of 42 to 26, that the Stadtholderate should be empowered to submit to the instructions of the Federal Commissaries, but on condition that the border fortresses of Rendsburg and Freiericsort should still be held by Schleswig-Holstein troops. No such condition can, of course, be admitted, for the dissolution of the insurrectionary army ts, next to that of the Stadtliolderate itself, the most important object to be effected. As a considerable portion of this army consists of German adventurers, who have found their way to IIolstein after having been repulsed in every other part of their own country, some alarm has been caused by the prospect of disbanding such a body of soldiers of tortune. Those who are not natives of the Duchies must be removed with despatch from the territory they have invaded in these free bands, and we believe 'hat the Hanoverian Government has guarded itself against their incursions

by providing a military escort on the frontier which will convey tliem back to their respective domiciles. Tins foreign clement being got rid of, the population of the Duchies will, wc believe, willingly return to their allegiance, and welcome tiie restoration of peace. The German writers who even at this extremity, have not lost their taste for fictitious encouragements, and who still obstinately resist the remonstrances of cians, sent out by Government to Jamaiill Europe and the positive demonstration of facts, have, at last, indulged their readers with an assurance that Lord Palmerston has protested against the advance of the Federal forces into Holstein. In this country it must be entirely superfluous to give to that assertion, a peremptory contradiction. þÿ The British Government lias formally ulopted the principle laid down by the Protocol of London : and wc venture to affirm that Lord Palincrston views with particular satisfaction an occurrence which must restore peace to the North of Europe, avert the danger of a Rns- >1.111 intervention, and relieve the Foreignoffice from one of the most wearisome md ungrateful tasks which ever devolved upon it. Hie deplorable contests, and the abortive schemes, of which the Sehleswig-IIolstein campaigns were the most protracted, if not the most conspicuous symptoms, will not he altogether lost ipon the German people if tlicy will have the candour to accept a lesson impressed upon them by so much utter

(Qai'D I AllS disappointment. It is the fashion with most of their literary agitators to quote the opinion and expressions of this journal, only for the purpose of denouncing our total blindness and incompetency to treat of German affairs; and we readily admit that there is much in the national mode of conducting their public business, which may in other countries pass for incomprehensible. But on looking back to the principal questions which it has been our lot to argue with our quick-sighted opponents, the result shows that there is not only not one of them on which we have been in the wrong, hut not one in which they have been right. The Frankfort Parliament, the dissolution of the Austrian Empire, the Prussian Union, the Three Kings League and the annexation of Schleswig to ilolstein, have been their grand þÿobjects all confidently predicted, all tenaciously pursued. Where are they now '/ Of which of them does any trace remain, except that humiliation which does follow a detected imposture, however people may affect to throw it off? Put this is not all. The false promises and misguided efforts oi a party utterly unable to accomplish any part oi what it attempted have not only in every instance failed, hut they have cast back the work oi constitutional government and liberal institutions throng out Germany. It is not our part, in commenting on the affairs of another country, to which we wish all freedom, prosperity, and power, to add anything to its own experience of the true state of its affairs ;

hut, as dispassionate spectators ot the condition of Germany, we may express the hope that this experience will carry with it some valuable hints and warnings for the future. þÿ Evening Mail, January 15.

Accordingly, the efforts of Prussian envoys and federal commissioners were as fruitless as the sermons ot the itinerant preachers of the Peace Society. But the renewed harmony between the cabinets of Vienna and Berlin, joined to the interest taken by the Emperor oj Russia in the Vanish questions has led to titrusurcs for pit tug effeel to the protocol of Ijondon. I rom the Alta California, Jan. 1.) .since our last monthly summary we have no stiring events to notice. We have, however, one item as pleasant to send to our friends in the States, as gratifying to us to be enabled to record. It is the entire cessation of the cholera. At one time it threatened us amazingly ; but it lias passed away, not only from San Francisco, but also from Sacramento City, where it raged most severely for a while. Wc do not hear of its ravages to any extent elsewhere in the country. The health ol' our State is excellent, not exceeded, we venture to assert, by any land on earth. There have been a number of society celebrations, which have helped bind together still stronger the tics of friendship and memory which conduce so m ich to individual happiness and social enjoyment. Another newspaper lias so been added to our corps in this c:ty.

<0 at <© AT S 3 one more in Sacramento, one in San Jose, and another about coming out þÿ The question of who shall be our next " U. S. Senator P' lias been considerably discussed ; but we are decidedly of opinion that the safest time for answering will be after the Legislature have balloted. The good old custom of Thanksgiving has been duly observed, and many a happy association awakened thereby. 4 Pilgrims' Day' was also celebrated by the Sons of New England and their o guests, ' in honor of the band who stood upon the shore of Plymouth two hundred and thirty years ago. This is well. We should cherish their memories and their virtues, and avoid their faults. Much anxiety is felt about the Panama steamer, over due here now for more than a week. But we hope her detention is nothing more than what may have resulted irom injury to her machinery, and that we shall ere long have the extreme pleasure of announcing her arrival. A number of our most prominent men have died during the month. Very suddenly were some of them called away, and at onotiine our city appeared reallv gloomy in consequence, lint a different feeling exists at present. There has been no small degree ol dissatisfaction expressed on account of an opinion from the Supreme Court, which goes to vitiate almost all the land titles in this city. A number of Steamers have arrived Irom around the lloru þÿ among others the Gen. Warren, Constitution, Ac. Our steam marine is increasing rapidly. The Koman Catholic Bishop ot California,

Dr. Alemaui, has arrived, aud received a most cheering welcome. Our business men have awakened to the importance ol the tine tield opened lor whaling from this port, as the emporium. F nl'ortunately, the tirst vessel lilted out lor that business, the Popmuu net, has been lost, with a part of her crew. Another vessel lias also been lost, but happily no iives lost, Report lroni the mines have been rather scarce, most of those engaged on the rivers during the summer, having gone into the dry diggings, from w horn a good account is anticipated next spring. Another large lire has visited us, but its ravages are so little, compared with previous ones þÿ only about 800,000 that it lias scarcely been noticed, except by the unfortunate sufferers. A part of Capt. French's company has arrived here. This will be pleasing news to their friends in the States. One of the heaviest gales that has been known for years, has raged on our coast and over the country. But the damage has not been very great þÿ the most unfortunate effects ot it yet known, being the loss ot the British ship Mersey, at the mouth of this bay. Our chief subject of discussion here in the city recently, in addition to the balls, lias been the medals ordered by somebody who seems not yet anxious to own up to the paternity, as a testimony of respect from everybody who knew nothing of the matter. <0 everybody else, including

the Aldermen. These medals will likely be to tliem what those conferred upon the French soldier? ' Rome were considered by the e troops a mark of dis- þÿ grace And so they are. þÿ New York Weekly Ileraul, l\b. 8.

ST. CROIX AVIS. Christiansted, 24th February, 1851. ON Friday morning last, the Schooner Vigilant, in attempting to clear the mouth of the harbour, was dismasted by the severe squall that occurred about half past 8 o'clock. By the same squall one of our fishing boats was upset and a fisherman drowned ; and on Saturday night about half past eleven, lire was discovered in the interior of the Secretary's Office at Government- House ; but by the truly praiseworthy exertions of the Brand Corps and Inhabitants in general, it was extinguished in about two hours front the first alarm : the women evinced much laborious zeal, and their exertions merit all praise. We regret, however, to state that a part of the Archives of the Ollice is very much damaged. Towards morning there were two shocks of an Earthquake; and another, very severe one, tit about halt past three, at which time a brilliant meteor was observed bv several persons.

SCIILESW IG ilOL,STEIN. Our advices by telegraph from Hamburg are of the 2i)th iust. A corps of 2,000 Austriuns entered Hamburg on that day. The new Government for Holstcin was to enter upon its functions on the 1st of February. The cabinet is composed ot Messrs. Blohtnc, Heintze, Malmros, and Prelui. The Kiilner Ztilung states that Rendslnirg is likely to become a Federal fortress. Our Hamburg correspondent confirms the statements of the German papers, which announce that the negotiations respecting the formation of a provisional government for Hoistein have been brought to a successful issue. The new Government of Hoistein will consist ot the Federal and Danish Commissioners, who will be supported by a council of the chief noblemen and moderate-minded landed proprietors of the duchy. Our correspondent informs us that the delay in this long-protracted negotiation has been owing to the underhand intrigues of the Prussian Commissioners. It has, however, at length been arranged that Frcdcrichsort is to be given up to the Danish troops, which will also occupy tin- positions north of

ltendsburg, while the small island which lies between those positions and the fortress, will, for the present, receive no garrison whatever. © Sicilian and Brazilian agents are on the alert to enlist the soldiers and Serjeants who arc being dismissed from the Holstcin army. The frost basset in at Hamburg, and the steamers plying between that city and London and Hull, have proceeded to Glnckstadt, where they will ship their mails and cargoes. The Borsenhalle states, from Schwerin, that in spite of the late protests of the Government, a force of 4,000 Austriaus will he quartered upon the Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg. þÿ Evening Mail. DENMARK AND HOI.STE1N. According to the Danish papers the King of Denmark has directed an intnn diatc exchange of all prisoners of war made during the iast campaign in Hoistein. It is reported also that the officers of the Ilolstein army, who were previous to the outbreak ot the war in the Danish service, and who consequent ly broke their oaths of allegiance bv serving against him, will he banished for ever from Ihe Danish þÿdominions. Captain Jesse, an officer who stood it: this position and was wounded and taker at the battle of Idstedt, has been broke by a court martial and sentenced to the same exile ; he litis received 100 tlialerv as travelling money, and was released from arrest on condition of leaving the kingdom. It was for some time believed in Hoistein that lie had been executed. Eighty soldiers dismissed from the llolsteiu army refused on the 20th to leave Rendsburg for Sclilesvvig, their place of settlement ; the officer finally satisfied them that they had nothing to apprehend from the llanish authorities ; and they left for the north. It is reported that some of the German Governments, and even that of Prussia, have re-considered the plan for raising a German free corps for the Brazils, as it would absorb many of the disbanded troops from Hoistein, who are likely to give great trouble when finally dispersed. It is added that no open op position will he made to the enlistment of the men ; it is mentioned as likely too that General Gcrhardt, late commander of the Avant-Guard of the Hoi-

stein army will enter the Brazilian service. He has lost his Prussian pension bv joining the army ot the Stathalterschafit ; and as lie quitted it without leave he has lost all claim on the Du chies ; he is therefore driven to this course by necessity. þÿ Ibid.

ANECDOTE. The following adventure given by a correspondent writing from Buffalo, actually took place in the town of M , in Ohio, a few years ago. Jt would have made even the late Isaac Hicks laugh at the solemn meeting on the seventh day. Farmer had two daughters, very interesting young Indies, yet in their teens, who were quite romantic in their notions. Their father was an aristocratic member of the Baptist church, and of course was very scrupulous as to the " company" his girls shall "keep" Now it happened that these two pretty girls became acquainted with a couple of young bucks, tradesmen in an adjoining village, arid to use a common expression, "took quite a shine to ' em.' " To this the old gentleman was very much opposed, as he had intended to match his daughters himself. But 'twas 110 use talking to them, while, week after week wore away, and found the young men constant visiters. At length, in order to force obedience the old man found himself driven to the necessity of locking up the foolish children who had presumed to fall in love with a couple of tradesmen. The sweet girls were accordingly confined on Sunday afternoons in the second story, which fronted the barn-yard, a very romantic "lookout." Under the window was a pile of stones, which had been left after repairing the cellar wall in that coiner. For three successive Sabbath evenings, the lovers had climbed by means of the sheets of the bed, which were let down from the window by the heroic girls, up to t he apartment

of the imprisoned lovers, and from nightfall until rosy morn did revel in the " ambrosial delight of love's young dream." But this clandestine courtship could not long he continued and not he discovered. One lovely Sabbath, just at twilight, the father coming from the barn thought he saw something rather ominous hanging out of the back window, so lie noiselessly walked around to ascertain tlm " nature" of it. There bung the fatal " fiag of surrender," and t he old man giving it a slight jerk commenced the ascent. He was lifted from off his feet, and felt himself gradually ' rising in the world.' 'Tvvas a heavy weight the daughters thought þÿ and to tell the truth it was a heavy " body corporate" at which they were hopefully tugging away. But lo ! his head had lust reached the window sill and just as his old white hat appeared above the window, his affectionate daughters " dropped him like a hot potatoe," and with something like the emphasis of " a squashed apple dumpling," the old man came in instant contact with the mother earth, while the two tape and scissors, who were not far off enjovirig the scone, "made hasty tracks" from the settlement, leaving nothing hehind tlicni but bodily misery, horror stricken damsels, and their own coat tails streaming on the cool night air. þÿ kitick eUo.h r.

What a Wife siioi i.o Do. þÿ " A wife must learn ii>vv to form her husband's happiness, 1.1 what direction the secret of ids comfort lies; she must not cherish his weakness 1 working upon them, she must not ra-.dy run counter to his prejudices. Her motto must be, never to irritate. She must study never to draw largely upon the small stock of patience in man's nature ; not lo increase his ob-

stinacy by trying to drive him : never, if Christians!. ,1 ; for price and conditions possible, to have scenes. 1 doubt much if a real quarrel, even if made up, does not loosen the bond between man and wife, and sometimes, unless the affection of both be very sincere, lastingly. If irritation should occur, a woman must expect to hear from most men a strength and vehemence of language far more than the occasion requires. Mild as well as stern men are prone to this exaggeration of language : let not a woman be tempted ever to say anything sarcastic or violent in retaliation. " The interior of the island ol'Chusan is remarkably beautiful and picturesque, and no part is more beautiful than the long valley, christened by Europeans 'Anstruther's Valley,' as it was there that officer fell into the hands of the Chinese. One of the most extraordinary circumstances connected with Captain Anstruther's capture is the following : those who believe in dreams, and that ' coming events east their shadows before,' will, by this recital, have that belief strengthened. The night before the captain was missed, a brother officer, in passing near his tent, heard moans, and suppressed groans of agony. An- -truther was awaked by his friend, who inquired what was the matter; the reply w as that he had dreamed that the Chinese had surrounded linn and made him a prisoner, whilst he was on tmaking a survey. Anstruther laughed, thanked Iks triend for looking in to see what was the matter, and wished him good nicht ; his friend returned the salutation, hied oil' to the mess to tell Anstruther's dream ; and many a hearty guffaw was indulged in at the captain's vision. " The following day, the 16th of September, Captain Anstruther went out to take a survey in the island, accompanied by an old lasear (who was the captain's faithful servant), both being, as usual, unarmed. Captain Vnstruther was taken prisoner by the Chinese, and the poor old faithful lascar w as butchered before his master's face."

The following extract affords at once a description of Chusan. and a general idea of Chinese scenery. The island is twenty-live miles long, and ten in width, .1 ml is nine miles distant from the main land of China : þÿ " In the island there are seventeen principal villages, together with many mailer ones or hamlets; these are tilled with well-cultivated farms, as but a small part of the fertile island of Cliu- :in is allowed to remain uncultivated; noble hills, front eight hundred to two thousand feet in height, which are frequently planted with fir and bamboos, meet the eye; whilst in the luxuriant valleys at their base grow paddy, beans, sweet potatoes, and maize ; and the lowlands are also adorned and enriched by the magnificent walnut, Spanish chestnut, varnish, and tallow trees. The farmers cultivate and raise cotton for their own use, a species of palm-tree is also reared on the side of the hills, from the fibre of which rope is made; and the green-tea tree is cultivated by all those who possess a farm, however small. As soon as the last crop of rice is got in, then the ground is prepared for the reception of other crops, such as cabbages, trefoil or clover, and the oil plant ; in short, almost all that grow, in China appears to he cultivated, and thrive in the fertile, beauteous island of Chusau. She was tenderly attached to every member of her family, and when the preliminaries of her marriage w ith Napoleon were arranged, and she knew that she was about to leave all who were so dear to her, and with whom she had passed all her days, her heart sunk within her, and her tears flowed incessantly. The day came : she was to leave forever the home of her childhood. She took a most affecting leave of all her family and then shut herself up in her own apartment, where, according to etiquette, she was to remain till the French embassador who was to conduct her to Paris went to hand Iicr to the carriage. The Liverpool "Sailors Home" was opened on the l(5tli December last, in clue form. The eholera has much abated in Norway and Sweden. Up to the 15th December, no new eases had been reported. It is proposed to erect a monument in Eiiinl rgh to Wallace, the Scotch hero. A great chess match, to be played by amateurs of all nations during the Exhibition of 1851, is being arranged for. In immense layer of sulphur has been discovered near Alexandria. It can be obtained in large quantities so cheaply, that it is expected the price of the article will be reduced in Europe. The landed interest of the late Sir Robert Peel was not much tinder £.'15,000 a year. ft i-» stated that about C70.000 was paid by the Government of Spain for the steamships llibernia and Caledonia. \ ii iron lighthouse of vast dimensions is about to be erected on the Eastnett, a solitary rock several miles out in the Mlantie, off the coast of Cork and Kerry. In London, under the patronage of the Lady Mayoress, a large carpet is in progress of preparation for the Exhibition. It is to be thirty feet in length, twenty in width, and to consist of one hundred and fifty squares. The foreign merchants and shippers of London have agreed to establish a "club for all nations," to meet the requirements of the strangers and others, wiio will be in town during the Exhibition of 1851. The club will be provided, in addition to the usual accommodations, with interpreters acquainted with all the languages of the East and of Europe,

guides and commissioners, and departments for information. A committee of gentlemen, merchants of London, has been elected to carry out the undertaking. The Koh-i-noor diamond, or Mountain of Light, will, it is said, he placed among the collection of minerals at the Exhibition in Hyde Park. \ new method of voting which oilers incontestable advantages on the score of accuracy and rapidity, has received an appropriation from the French Chambers. Each member is provided with a box containing ten ballots; five white (aye), and live blue ( my). These consist of oblong squares of steel, having the name of the representative engraved upon each side. The urns are soon arranged that the white and blue ballots fall into different compartments, not at random, but arrange themselves against a graduated copper rod, which shows at a glance the number of ballots for or against. These rods arc taken from the urns, and placed upon a piece of mechanism upon the tribune, so arranged that one side shows all the ayes, the other all the nays, and the secretaries have only to add up the sums of the rods. Then, by touching a lever, the sides are reversed, so that the secretaries who have added the ayes have the

3 O tR '® !t Z. nays presented to them ; thus mutually checking each other. The result is thus ascertained in a few minutes, with scarcely a possibility of error. Lists arc prepared before hand bearing numbers corresponding to those engraved on a corner of the ballots, by which means the copy for the Moniteur is speedily furnished with the utmost accuracy. þÿ This which used to take a considerable time, and swarmed with errors, can now be done in ten minutes. This ingenious and beautiful apparatus costs 27,000 francs.

A new aeronautic machine lias been exhibited at Paris, which it is claimed solves the long sought problem, at least on a small scale, of directing the course of a balloon through the air. The leading idea of the machine are drawn from the structure of birds and fishes, the animals that possess the power of traversing liquid a element. The model with which the successful experiments were performed, consists of a balloon of gold-beaters' skin, inflated with hydrogen, some three or four yards long, nearly round in front, and terminating in a horizontal rudder like the tail of a bird; a little before and above which is another rudder placed vertically, like the tail of a fish. The former is to change the course of the vessel up and down, the latter to turn it to the rignt or left. Toward the head of the balloon, in a position corresponding to that of the tins of a fish, are placed light wings, capable of a rapid motion, which constitute the motive power, in the model these are set in motion by machinery ; but in the working machine human power is proposed. A framework of hollow iron is placed horizontally around the balloon to which it is attached by cords; this furnishes the fixed point to which are attached the cords which move the rudders : and from it is suspended the car in w hich t lie passengers are to be placed. The inventor promises to construct a machine capable of carrying up fifty persons, lie acknowledges that the apparatus will be bulky, but consoles himself by the rellectiou that there

is no present danger of the air being crowded. The whole weight of the machine and its burden is to be so proportioned to the amount of hydrogen in the balloon, that it will remain in equilibrium ; an anchor is then to be thrown overboard, when the machine will of course rise ; when a sullicient height is gained the anchor is to be weighed, and the equilibrium being again restored, the machine will be stationary ; and it may then be propelled and guided by the wings and the rudders. Such, at least, is the belief of one of the editors of La Sicc/e, who was present at the trial of the model, and who indulges in the most glowing anticipations of the future success of the invention. Rossini is said to be secretly superintending, at lloulogne, the production of a musical work to which lie attaches great importance. Ho passes every evening and a part of each day with the Lunous tenor Donzelli, in revising this
work, which has not yet been made known to the public, and which, it is said, will soon be performed at Boulogne.

It is stated in the French journals that in consequence of the confusion existing between the maritime calculations of different powers, and the unfortunate occurrences to which it some times leads, the naval powers of the north þÿ Russia, Sweden, Denmark, and Holland have entered into an agreement, to open conferences on the old question of a common meridian for all nations. France, Spain, and Portugal, it is said, have given in their adhesion to the scheme ; and a hope is held out that England will come into the arrangement. The most advanced opinion on the Continent seems to be in favar of the selection of an entirely neutral point of intersection þÿ say Cape Horn þÿ which it is said would have the immense advantage being agreeable to the Americans. M. l'olain, keeper of the Archives at the famous French Liege, has recently discovered that historian, Froissart, w hose Chronicles are universally known, copied the first fifty chapters of his work, tioin Jelian le Eel, an author of his own time, whose manuscripts have been recently discovered in the llelgian libra-

ries. This is a discovery of considerable interest to antiquarians. An edition of one hundred and twenty-five copies ol Jeliau le Bel's book has been printed foe the use ol a select number of historical sa vans.

Schiavone who is quite celebrated for the skill wiih which he copies, 'l'ne Ex-Emperor of Austria, it is said, surprised to find, in one of his visits to Venice, that no monument had been erected to the memory of Titian, ordered, at his own expense, the construction of one worthy of the immortal painter, llo left to the Academy of Venice the choice of the form of the monument, and of the site on which it should be erected The Academy, after a discussion pro forma, confided the monument to one of its members, AL Z.indomcni, professor of sculpture. Now that the constitution of the Conference is known, the apprehension that it was to he a mere consultation of Princes and bureaux if more than confirmed. This, indeed, i<: the very purpose of the Conference, as expressed in the Austrian circular to the various Governments in Germany, just, published by The Vienna Gazette. The Conference is there stated to he one of " the representatives of all the German Governments," and it is charged with the revising of the fundamental laws of the Confederation. The Plenipotentiaries chosen are not only the ordinary servants of the Governments, hut they arc, in some cases, the pledged representatives of Absolutism. MIII.CSUIL IIOhSI'ElV, SUBMISSION OF THE STADTIIOL- DERS. The Times Office, Quarter past 12 p. m. Our advices by telegraph from Hamburg are to the 12th inst. The question of the Duchies isdccidcd. The Stadtholders have resolved to submit. On Saturday last the two Commissioners, General Thienen and Count Mensdorf, returned from Kiel to Hamburg.

At that time it was stated that they had effected an arrangement with the Stadtholders and Count R event low. The Holstein Diet had not, however, dissolved itself. Many of its members thought it advisable to proceed to Hamburg on Saturday night. It was rumoured that the march of the Austrian army would he stopped, and that the Holstein troops would remain in possession ofRendsburg. This report is,' however, contradicted by later intelligence, according to which the Stadtholders have published a proclamation, in which document they statu that, since the German Confederacy ha? resolved to enforce the treaty of peace of the 2d July 1850, and since that Confederacy has promised to protect the right of Holstein, as well as the vested right and ancient connexion existing between that duchy and Schleswig, they, the Stadtholders, had thought it incumbent on themselves to decree the cessation of hostilities. They finally protest that they have placed the right of the country under the protection of the Gei manic Confederation. Tiny a'so express their thanks to the army, the navy, and the population at large, and they rely on the maintenance of order The Stadtholders will resign then office as soon as an administrative board shall have been appointed by the Germanic < 'onfedcration. þÿ Evening þÿMai , !
